title: The Sixteenth Locker
premise: When sixteen-year-old Tamsin Okonkwo transfers to Hollowmere Academy, she's assigned to locker sixteen — the one that shouldn't exist, opening onto a stairwell the blueprints say isn't there. Paired with her nemesis, golden-boy Declan Voss, for a history project on the school's founding, they discover the building was raised in 1962 over a shuttered orphanage whose sixteen residents vanished the night of a fire. The lockers are doors into the orphans' final day, replaying on a loop, and each visit erases a piece of the visitor's own memory. As Tamsin and Declan piece together the cover-up — the school board's founding families burned the orphanage for the land — they realize Tamsin's missing childhood memories and the orphans' disappearance are the same story, and that the loop is consuming her identity. To end it, Tamsin must choose: restore her own past by walking away, or surrender her memories entirely to carry the sixteen children out of the fire and into being remembered. She chooses the children, and the final chapter shows a school where locker sixteen is just a locker — and a memorial plaque, newly installed, bearing sixteen names and hers.
about_author: Tamsin Whitlock is a former school archivist who spent three years cataloguing a condemned building's records and never quite shook the feeling that some of them were still warm. She writes young adult fiction about places that remember what people would rather forget, and lives in a coastal town with too many locked doors.

chapters.title: Fine, Obviously
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Three weeks into Hollowmere Academy, Tamsin narrates her aggressively ordinary new life while pointedly avoiding the question of what she's forgotten — her mother's face, her sixth birthday, whole years. Emotional beat: brittle denial, humor as armor, the reader sensing cracks beneath the 'fine.'

chapters.title: Locker Sixteen
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Assigned locker sixteen, Tamsin finds the number freshly painted over older, deeper numerals. When it sticks, the janitor pales and swaps it 'for maintenance' — but that night she dreams of a stairwell going down. Emotional beat: first unease, the ordinary world tilting one degree.

chapters.title: Assigned Partners
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. History teacher Ms. Ferro pairs Declan Voss — student council prince, keeper of the school's shiny founding myth — with Tamsin, the girl who publicly called his family's legacy 'a museum of lies.' Emotional beat: mutual loathing crackling with reluctant curiosity.

chapters.title: The Founders' Floor
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. Researching in the archive, they find the 1962 cornerstone photo: sixteen lockers in the basement, and a building beneath the building. Declan's family name is on every donor plaque. Emotional beat: the project stops being homework.

chapters.title: What the Blueprints Say Isn't There
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin sneaks into the sub-basement and finds the stairwell from her dream — and sixteen rusted lockers, one standing open, exhaling cold air that smells of smoke. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: Declan's Inheritance
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. Declan confronts his grandmother, who goes white at the word 'orphanage' and forbids him to dig. He digs. He finds a sealed board minute from 1962, redacted to ribbons. Emotional beat: a golden boy's faith in his family cracking.

chapters.title: The First Loop
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Locker sixteen at the school opens onto the stairwell; inside, Tamsin witnesses a looped fragment — a girl in a 1962 nightgown counting children, sixteen of them, as smoke blooms at a doorway that never quite arrives. Tamsin wakes with a nosebleed and one fewer memory of her mother. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into cost.

chapters.title: Comparing Wounds
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Forced into honesty by evidence, Tamsin and Declan trade what they've lost and learned: her missing years, his redacted minutes, the loop's rules — each visit takes something. Emotional beat: enemies becoming co-conspirators, trust built from shared damage.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Counts
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Deeper in the loop, Tamsin meets the counting girl — Ada — who recognizes her, calls her by a name that isn't Tamsin Okonkwo's, and begs her to 'stop the bell.' Emotional beat: the mystery turns personal and terrifying.

chapters.title: Board of Silence
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. Declan and Tamsin crash a school board reception; his grandmother publicly humiliates Tamsin, and Declan defects to her side in front of everyone. Emotional beat: Declan burning his old life for the truth.

chapters.title: Sixteen Names, None Spoken
chapters.summary: Both POVs. In the county records hall they recover the orphanage ledger: sixteen children, and a fire ruled accidental the same night the land sold. One name matches Tamsin's forgotten middle name. Emotional beat: vertigo — she isn't investigating the past, she's inside it.

chapters.title: The Bell Rings Both Ways
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The loop begins bleeding into school days: fire alarms with no fire, classmates humming a lullaby no one taught them. Tamsin loses another memory — her best friend's face — and realizes she has maybe three visits left before there's no 'her' left. Emotional beat: racing against her own erasure.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Buried
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. Declan's grandmother, dying, confesses: her father lit the fire to force the orphanage's sale; the children died because the doors were locked from outside. She gives him the original key. Emotional beat: generational guilt laid bare; the weapon and the burden, handed over.

chapters.title: The Fourteenth Visit
chapters.summary: Both POVs. They map all sixteen lockers as loop-doors and plan a single run: unlock the dormitory door inside the loop before the fire reaches it. But Ada warns them the loop protects itself — and something in the smoke has started protecting it back. Emotional beat: dread and resolve in equal measure.

chapters.title: Everything Tamsin Kept
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Before the final run, Tamsin writes down every memory she has left and mails the letter to herself, so that whoever wakes up will know who she was. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; identity as a letter to a stranger.

chapters.title: Into the Fire, Again
chapters.summary: Both POVs. They enter the loop at its worst moment — the night of the fire itself — and move through smoke and screaming history, unlocking doors, counting children aloud as the loop fights back with their own erased memories used against them. Emotional beat: the climax's first half — courage, chaos, sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Bell
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Ada refuses to leave without the last child, who is Tamsin — the sixteenth, the one who escaped the fire but not the memory of it, the source of her missing years. To free them all, Tamsin must give the loop her remaining self. Emotional beat: the choice made plain; she chooses the children.

chapters.title: Sixteen Out
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The children cross out of the loop as the fire finally, mercifully, completes — and Tamsin stands in the white heat, letting go. Declan drags her body from locker sixteen as the stairwell collapses into ordinary concrete. Emotional beat: climax resolved in grief and grace.

chapters.title: The Girl in the Infirmary
chapters.summary: Declan's POV. Tamsin wakes with no memories at all, holding a letter addressed in her own handwriting. Declan reads it to her, then tells her the truth of everything, including what she gave up. Emotional beat: quiet devastation, and the first fragile question — can identity be rebuilt from testimony and love?

chapters.title: What the Board Cannot Bury
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The ledger, the key, the confession, and the recovered names go public. The board resigns; the founding families' plaques come down; Declan's grandmother's confession is read aloud at the hearing. Emotional beat: justice as exposure — the theme of power's corruption answered with record-keeping and witness.

chapters.title: Sixteen Names, and Hers
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At the memorial's unveiling, sixteen names are read, then a seventeenth: Tamsin Okonkwo, 'who carried them out.' She doesn't remember doing it — but she chooses to believe the girl in the letter. Emotional beat: identity re-chosen rather than remembered.

chapters.title: Locker Sixteen
chapters.summary: Both POVs, closing. Months later: locker sixteen opens on textbooks, nothing else. Ada's lullaby is taught in music class, credited. Tamsin and Declan, no longer enemies, add a new page to the school archive — and Tamsin writes the first line of a story she'll never remember living. Emotional beat: bittersweet peace; memory survives as story, identity as choice.
